name: Postcentral gyrus (primary somatosensory cortex)
func: The strip just behind the central sulcus where body sensations first reach the cortex: touch, pressure, vibration, joint position, pain and temperature. Each part maps a body part on the opposite side.

levels.kid:
Right behind the "move" strip in your brain is the **feeling strip**. Scientists call it the **sensory cortex**.

When a bug lands on your arm, tiny sensors in your skin send a message up to this strip, and a spot on it says, "Hey, something is on the arm!" That is how you know where you were touched.

Just like the move strip, it is crossed: the left side of your brain feels the right side of your body.

Your fingertips and lips get big spots because they are super sensitive. That is why you can read tiny bumps with your fingers, but your back can hardly tell whether one pencil or two pencils is poking it.
levels.hs:
The **postcentral gyrus** is the first ridge of the **parietal lobe**, lying directly behind the **central sulcus**. In front of it, across the sulcus, is the precentral gyrus (primary motor cortex), and behind it is the postcentral sulcus and the rest of the parietal lobe. Like the motor strip, it runs from the top of the brain down to the lateral fissure and continues onto the medial surface in the paracentral lobule.

It is the **primary somatosensory cortex (S1)**. Signals from receptors in the skin, muscles and joints travel up the spinal cord and brainstem, cross to the opposite side, relay in the **thalamus**, and arrive here. So the left S1 receives sensation from the right side of the body.

The body is laid out as a **sensory homunculus**, very similar to the motor map: the leg and foot on the medial surface, then trunk, arm, hand, face and, at the bottom near the lateral fissure, the lips, tongue and throat. The fingertips and lips have huge areas because they are packed with receptors. You can test this with **two-point discrimination**: a fingertip can tell apart two points a few millimeters apart, while the back needs several centimeters.
levels.college:
S1 consists of **Brodmann areas 3a, 3b, 1 and 2**, arranged in strips from the depth of the central sulcus back to the crest and posterior slope of the gyrus:

- **3a** (deep in the sulcus): proprioception from muscle spindles.
- **3b**: light touch and texture; this is "S1 proper," with the sharpest map.
- **1**: texture.
- **2**: size and shape, combining touch and joint position.

Input comes from the **ventral posterolateral (VPL)** nucleus of the thalamus for the body and the **ventral posteromedial (VPM)** nucleus for the face. These relay two main pathways: the **dorsal column-medial lemniscus** system (fine touch, vibration, proprioception), which crosses in the medulla, and the **spinothalamic (anterolateral)** system (pain, temperature, crude touch), which crosses in the spinal cord. Facial sensation arrives through the trigeminal system.

S1 sends output to the **secondary somatosensory cortex (S2)** in the parietal operculum along the upper bank of the lateral fissure, to the superior parietal lobule (areas 5 and 7) for body schema and reaching, and directly to motor cortex. It also sends descending fibers in the corticospinal tract that modulate sensory relay in the dorsal horn.

Blood supply matches the motor strip: the **ACA** supplies the medial leg area and the **MCA** supplies the lateral face and arm areas.

Pain is not processed in S1 alone. Its location and intensity involve S1 and S2, while its unpleasantness relies on the anterior cingulate and the insula.
levels.phd:
Vernon Mountcastle discovered in the 1950s that S1 is built from **cortical columns**: vertical groups of neurons spanning all layers that share the same receptive-field location and the same receptor type. This columnar principle became a foundational idea for the whole neocortex.

Thalamic axons end mainly in **layer IV**, onto spiny stellate cells, which pass signals up to layers II/III and then down to layer V output neurons. Receptive fields grow larger and more complex from area 3b to 1 and 2: 3b neurons respond to a small skin patch, while area 2 neurons respond to stimuli across several fingers and to particular edge orientations or directions of motion.

In rodents, the whisker part of S1 forms **barrel cortex**, in which each whisker maps to a visible cluster of cells in layer IV. Barrel cortex is one of the most important models for studying how experience shapes cortical circuits.

S1 maps are **plastic**. Merzenich and Kaas showed that after a monkey loses input from a finger, neighboring finger areas expand into the silent territory. In people after arm amputation, the face area can invade the former hand area, which relates to **phantom limb** sensations, where touching the face is felt on the missing hand (Ramachandran). Practice expands representations: string players have enlarged maps for the fingers of the left hand.

S1 is also involved in action. **Sensorimotor integration** with motor cortex allows grip force to adjust within about 100 ms when an object starts to slip. In brain-computer interface research, **intracortical microstimulation** of S1 in people with spinal cord injury has produced sensations felt in specific fingers, restoring touch feedback to robotic arm control.
levels.expert:
A lesion of S1 produces **contralateral cortical sensory loss**. The hallmark is loss of **discriminative** sensation, while crude pain and temperature sense are relatively spared because they are partly perceived at the thalamic level. Classic **cortical sensory signs**, tested only when basic sensation is intact, include:

- **Astereognosis:** cannot identify an object such as a coin by touch with eyes closed.
- **Agraphesthesia:** cannot recognize numbers traced on the palm.
- **Impaired two-point discrimination.**
- **Sensory extinction:** the patient feels a touch on either side alone but misses the side opposite the lesion when both are touched at once (this also suggests parietal neglect).
- **Loss of position sense**, sometimes with "pseudoathetosis," where the outstretched hand writhes when the eyes are closed.

Because it sits next to the motor strip, a stroke or tumor here often causes combined weakness and sensory loss. MCA strokes affect the face and arm; ACA strokes affect the leg.

**Focal sensory seizures** begin with tingling or numbness that may march across the body like a Jacksonian motor seizure.

**Imaging:** MRI shows the postcentral gyrus behind the hand knob. In surgery, **somatosensory evoked potentials (SSEPs)** from the median nerve are recorded on the cortex: the waveform flips polarity (**phase reversal**) across the central sulcus, a reliable way to tell the motor strip from the sensory strip. Direct stimulation in awake patients causes tingling in a body part rather than movement.

Surgeons tend to accept small sensory deficits more readily than motor ones, but removing the hand area of S1 causes a clumsy hand even with normal strength, because fine motor control depends on sensory feedback. Spinal cord injury and peripheral nerve problems can mimic cortical sensory loss, so the examination localizes the lesion before imaging.

keyPoints: Postcentral gyrus = first gyrus of the parietal lobe, behind the central sulcus
Receives from the thalamus: VPL (body) and VPM (face)
Sensory homunculus: leg medial, face lateral; big hands and lips
Lesion → astereognosis, agraphesthesia, poor two-point discrimination
SSEP phase reversal finds the central sulcus in surgery

test.q: Which thalamic nucleus relays touch from the face to S1?
test.explain: VPM carries trigeminal input from the face; VPL carries input from the body.

test.q: Inability to identify a coin by touch alone, with normal basic sensation, is called ______.
test.explain: Astereognosis is a cortical sensory sign of parietal/S1 damage.

test.q: Which Brodmann area of S1 lies deepest in the central sulcus and handles proprioception?
test.explain: Area 3a receives muscle spindle input and lies in the depth of the central sulcus.

test.q: After arm amputation, touching the face can be felt on the missing hand because:
choices: The face area expands into the former hand area of S1
test.explain: Cortical maps reorganize; the face area sits next to the hand area on the homunculus.

test.q: The vertical groups of neurons sharing the same receptive field, discovered by Mountcastle, are called cortical ______.
test.explain: Mountcastle described columnar organization in S1.

test.q: The intraoperative test that shows a waveform flip across the central sulcus uses:
test.explain: Median nerve SSEPs reverse polarity across the central sulcus.
